title: Calling someone ‘nice’ once meant they were foolish
body: ‘Nice’ comes from Latin nescius, ‘not knowing’, and reached English through Old French, where it meant simple or foolish. Over the centuries it drifted to ‘fussy’, then ‘delicate’, then ‘precise’, a sense that survives in ‘a nice distinction’, before meaning ‘agreeable’ by the 1760s and ‘kind’ by the 1830s. Linguists call this semantic change: a word keeps its form while its meaning wanders.
